name: Ten-step Korean routine

lead: The ten-step Korean routine is a skincare regimen from South Korean beauty culture. It layers cleansing, toning, essence, treatment, mask, moisturiser and sunscreen, aiming for hydrated, even, glowing-looking skin.

It spread widely in the West in the 2010s via the Korean Wave, K-dramas and online tutorials. The routine is a cultural framework rather than a single studied protocol, and people shorten or adapt it.

paras: A typical description starts with a double cleanse (oil-based then water-based), followed by steps such as exfoliation, toner, essence, serum or ampoule, sheet mask, eye cream, moisturiser and, by day, sunscreen. At night a heavier sleep cream may replace sunscreen. Followers often use it daily and adjust steps to their skin.

More products means more chances of irritation or allergy for some skin types, and ingredients vary by brand. Dermatology clinics generally advise matching products to skin type; this is attributed guidance, not a rule of the routine.

chain: Skin barrier kept moisturised and protected from sun
angle.text: The routine aims at hydrated, even-looking skin through consistent cleansing, moisturising and sun protection, with some brands adding brightening ingredients.

lead: The ten-step Korean routine is a multi-stage skincare regimen associated with K-beauty, the umbrella term for South Korean skincare. It typically begins with a double cleanse and continues through products such as essences, serums, sheet masks and moisturiser, ending with sunscreen in the morning or a sleep cream at night, to achieve hydrated, brighter-looking skin.[1]

K-beauty draws on a long Korean beauty culture in which fair, clear skin was prized, and it grew in the West through the Korean Wave, K-drama product tie-ins, YouTube tutorials and duty-free sales.[1] BB cream reached Western markets around 2011, and a 2014 drama sponsorship by Amorepacific was reported to coincide with large sales rises.[1]
The routine is promoted by brands and influencers; no clinical trial of the ten-step routine as a whole has been published.

paras: Descriptions list roughly ten steps: double cleanse, sheet masks, essences, lotions, serums, moisturisers and, in the daytime, SPF 35 sunscreen, with a thicker sleep cream at night. Products often feature ingredients such as green tea, snail secretion, bee venom and collagen.[1]

Early Korean cosmetics used oils, plants and powders, and beauty culture grew during the Three Kingdoms period and peaked in the Goryeo era. Under the Joseon dynasty, fair skin and cherry lips signified status.[1] Modern global interest followed the Korean Wave and celebrity endorsement, with Mintel reporting about 68 percent of skincare launches coming from South Korea at one point.[1]
Critics in South Korea, such as the 2018 Escape the Corset movement reported by The New York Times, challenge rigid beauty standards and attitudes to cosmetic surgery.[1]
